# Technip Energies (TE.PA) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee · price used €29.90 (Euronext Paris close, 2026-08-02) · continuation of coverage begun 2026-07-27*

Technip Energies is a French-listed engineering and construction (E&C) company that designs and builds large energy plants — liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, offshore production units, and increasingly carbon-capture and low-carbon-fuel facilities. It runs two segments: Project Delivery (the big lump-sum construction projects) and Technology, Products & Services, or TPS (higher-margin proprietary technology, equipment, catalysts and consulting). It carries a large net-cash balance sheet and a backlog worth roughly three years of revenue.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across the eight quarters from the full-year 2024 call (2025-02-27) to the first-half 2026 call (2026-07-30), the story travelled through three distinct chapters.

**Chapter one — the confident growth story (early-to-mid 2025).** Management opened 2025 leading with a "€8.6 billion revenue, €800 million EBITDA by 2028" road map, an "all-time-high backlog approaching €20 billion," and a "near 50% increase in annual dividend." The emphasis was offensive: order intake over €10 billion for two straight years, a €75 billion commercial pipeline, and a new third leg (Reju, textile-to-textile recycling) framed as optional long-term upside.

**Chapter two — quiet de-risking under a worsening macro (mid-to-late 2025).** The tone stayed confident but the language turned more defensive. Management "widened the revenue range" for the shorter-cycle TPS segment "just in case," citing "delays in some of the carbon capture decisions… related to geopolitical events." Green hydrogen was downgraded from a growth driver to "a bit of a disappointment… slow to take off." The company leaned harder on the two durable pillars — Project Delivery's multi-year backlog coverage and TPS margin expansion — and made its first acquisition (Ecovyst's Advanced Materials & Catalysts, or AM&C, closed 2025-12-31) to add recurring, consumable catalyst revenue.

**Chapter three — the war shock (2026).** The full-year 2025 call (2026-02-26) was a high-water mark: record €7.2 billion revenue and €638 million EBITDA, a €1.00 dividend (+18%), a €150 million buyback, and the marquee North Field West (NFW) LNG award in Qatar. Then the first-half 2026 call (2026-07-30) delivered the sharp break: revenue held flat at €3.7 billion, but recurring EBITDA fell about a third to €212 million, and Project Delivery EBITDA dropped 45% to a 4.3% margin because the prolonged Middle East conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz drove up logistics, safety and business-continuity costs and forced provisions against seven disputed contract items. Management cut Project Delivery's full-year margin guidance to "5% plus" (from around 8%). The offsetting headline was extraordinary: €12.7 billion of first-half orders (a book-to-bill of about 3.4) lifting backlog to a record €25 billion.

The through-line: the long-term franchise story has actually *strengthened* (record backlog, diversification away from the Middle East, TPS quality), while the near-term earnings base took a genuine, exogenous hit.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Strong balance sheet… significant net cash" (every call) | Gross cash €4.8bn at mid-2026, but this sits against €4.1bn of customer advances (net contract liabilities). Management itself publishes the honest figure: economic net cash of roughly €900 million–€1 billion. | **Verified, with a caveat.** The often-quoted ~€2.9bn optical net cash triple-counts customer money; the real, unencumbered figure is ~€900M. Management is unusually candid about this. |
| "€800 million EBITDA by 2028… we are slightly ahead" | 2025 recurring EBITDA €638M (+5%). 2026 will fall well short after the war hit. Management reaffirms 2028 as "absolutely compatible." | **Credible but now war-contingent.** The trajectory was on track pre-conflict; the 2028 target survives only if the Middle East normalizes and cost recovery lands. |
| "Best-in-class Project Delivery margins" | Segment EBITDA margin ran ~8% through 2024-25, then collapsed to 4.3% in H1 2026. | **Broke on an exogenous shock, not on execution.** The cause is Hormuz logistics and provisions, and the rest of the (non-Middle-East) portfolio "is absolutely delivering." |

Where the story is *richer than the numbers*: the 2028 €800M EBITDA target and 2027 "meaningful recovery." Where it is *poorer than the numbers suggest at a glance*: the optical net cash and free-cash-flow yield, which are inflated by customer advances.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable, with a defensive shift in the near term.**

- FY2024 (2025-02-27): peak confidence — "outstanding," "stellar," "highest-ever," near-50% dividend hike. Offensive.
- Q1 2025 (2025-04-30): still confident but hedging — "we have widened the revenue range… considering some of the macro movements… just in case."
- H1/9M 2025: measured; leaning on backlog coverage and TPS margins; green hydrogen openly labelled "a bit of a disappointment."

- H1 2026 (2026-07-30): candid and defensive — "clearly disappointing," "we acknowledge the setback," repeated insistence on being "nonspeculative and prudent." ---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** The company confirmed its full-year 2025 guidance at every 2025 call and delivered a record year. - **Cost-recovery quantum and timing** (Rothschild, Kepler, Morgan Stanley, H1 2026): analysts pressed repeatedly for how much of the €30-40 million-per-quarter logistics hit is recoverable and when. - **Reju / adjacent bets**: analysts consistently probe the cash going into Reju; management caps it (~€50M/year) and frames it as optional.

The topic analysts pushed on that *became* the bad news: geopolitical/Middle East risk, flagged softly from Q1 2025, which detonated in H1 2026.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The near-term earnings base is hostage to one exogenous factor** — the Strait of Hormuz. Management's own base case assumes the disruption "persists throughout the year," and the top line could fall "if things were worsening."
🔴 **Cost recovery is real but undated and unsigned for the majority** — booked-at-cost even where signed (dilutive), and the "weeks to come" language has a whiff of the serially-deferred.
🔴 **Optical cheapness is misleading** — the ~€2.9bn net cash and ~25% free-cash-flow yield are inflated by customer advances; the honest figures (~€900M net cash) are far less dramatic.
🔴 **Higher tax rate (30-32%)** and elevated corporate costs (€65-70M) compress 2026 net income further.

🟢 **Record €25 billion backlog (+50% year-to-date), ~3x revenue** — the strongest visibility in company history, ~75% sourced outside the Middle East over 24 months.
🟢 **TPS margin at a record 15.4%** and structurally improving via AM&C (catalysts, ~70% OpEx-linked recurring revenue).
🟢 **Genuine net-cash balance sheet** funding a €1.00 dividend, a completed €150M buyback, and ~€300M of 2026 shareholder returns (~5% of market cap).
🟢 **Cash conversion held at 86%** through the profit trough.
🟢 **Management candour** — the war hit was owned, quantified where possible, and prudently provisioned.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **"Energy addition," not "energy transition."** The CEO's language has shifted toward energy security and supply diversification — "GCC countries… reducing reliance on the Strait of Hormuz… fast-tracking pipelines and export hubs." The war is being reframed as a *demand catalyst* for new infrastructure (alternative export routes, fast-track projects), which is where the €12.7bn order surge partly comes from.
- **Diversification is now the headline defence.** The "75% of orders outside the Middle East" statistic, once a footnote, is now the CEO's first answer to any Middle East risk question.
- **Capital allocation maturing.** From "dividend growth" (2024) to disciplined M&A (AM&C) plus a buyback plus a new €500M bond raised "for general corporate purposes" — the balance sheet is being put to work, not just admired.
- **A new adjacent bet appeared quietly:** a sustainable-aviation-fuel joint venture with Airbus, Safran and Tereos, sitting alongside Reju as optional long-term optionality.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.** The durable earnings engine is intact and, on the commercial side, stronger than ever; the 2026 profit shock is exogenous, transitory in management's framing, and backed by contractual cost-recovery rights and a fortress-adjacent (net-cash) balance sheet.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is, right now, a levered bet on the Strait of Hormuz reopening and on cost-recovery agreements getting signed. The recovery thesis is *not* independent of the single dominant macro factor the committee is most exposed to. The upside (a re-rate as margins normalize toward the reaffirmed €800M 2028 EBITDA framework) is real but undated; the downside is a war that drags into 2027 and keeps Project Delivery margins pinned near 5%. The discount to a fair reckoning of intrinsic value is only modest (~10-15%), so this is a quality franchise at a fair-to-slightly-cheap price with a live geopolitical overhang — not a deep, clean bargain.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trend STABLE.** The durable advantages are proprietary LNG and carbon-capture technology (intangible/IP), incumbency on the Qatar North Field complex (NFE/NFS/NFW) that compounds into follow-on awards, and a negative-working-capital model that makes the business self-funding. These are real but not impregnable — this is a competitive-bid E&C market (Saipem, Worley, KBR, Chiyoda, JGC). The core-margin compression is exogenous (war), not erosion; TPS margins are actually *widening*, which is why the moat trend is stable rather than eroding.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The obvious worry — a long-term decline in gas/LNG demand under the energy transition — cuts the other way here: Technip Energies is positioned as a transition *winner* (carbon capture, blue/green molecules, sustainable fuels, LNG as coal-displacement and data-center power). A 2028+ LNG oversupply is a cyclical risk to award timing, not a terminal-value threat to the franchise. The cheapness is therefore a fear-print around a war and a profit trough, not a structurally shrinking base — but the margin of safety is thin enough that discipline, not enthusiasm, is warranted.

# Technip Energies (TE.PA) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee · price used €29.90 (Euronext Paris close, 2026-08-02) · continuation of coverage begun 2026-07-27*

Technip Energies is a French-listed engineering and construction (E&C) company that designs and builds large energy plants — liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, offshore production units, and increasingly carbon-capture and low-carbon-fuel facilities. It runs two segments: Project Delivery (the big lump-sum construction projects) and Technology, Products & Services, or TPS (higher-margin proprietary technology, equipment, catalysts and consulting). It carries a large net-cash balance sheet and a backlog worth roughly three years of revenue.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across the eight quarters from the full-year 2024 call (2025-02-27) to the first-half 2026 call (2026-07-30), the story travelled through three distinct chapters.

**Chapter one — the confident growth story (early-to-mid 2025).** Management opened 2025 leading with a "€8.6 billion revenue, €800 million EBITDA by 2028" road map, an "all-time-high backlog approaching €20 billion," and a "near 50% increase in annual dividend." The emphasis was offensive: order intake over €10 billion for two straight years, a €75 billion commercial pipeline, and a new third leg (Reju, textile-to-textile recycling) framed as optional long-term upside.

**Chapter two — quiet de-risking under a worsening macro (mid-to-late 2025).** The tone stayed confident but the language turned more defensive. Management "widened the revenue range" for the shorter-cycle TPS segment "just in case," citing "delays in some of the carbon capture decisions… related to geopolitical events." Green hydrogen was downgraded from a growth driver to "a bit of a disappointment… slow to take off." The company leaned harder on the two durable pillars — Project Delivery's multi-year backlog coverage and TPS margin expansion — and made its first acquisition (Ecovyst's Advanced Materials & Catalysts, or AM&C, closed 2025-12-31) to add recurring, consumable catalyst revenue.

**Chapter three — the war shock (2026).** The full-year 2025 call (2026-02-26) was a high-water mark: record €7.2 billion revenue and €638 million EBITDA, a €1.00 dividend (+18%), a €150 million buyback, and the marquee North Field West (NFW) LNG award in Qatar. Then the first-half 2026 call (2026-07-30) delivered the sharp break: revenue held flat at €3.7 billion, but recurring EBITDA fell about a third to €212 million, and Project Delivery EBITDA dropped 45% to a 4.3% margin because the prolonged Middle East conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz drove up logistics, safety and business-continuity costs and forced provisions against seven disputed contract items. Management cut Project Delivery's full-year margin guidance to "5% plus" (from around 8%). The offsetting headline was extraordinary: €12.7 billion of first-half orders (a book-to-bill of about 3.4) lifting backlog to a record €25 billion.

The through-line: the long-term franchise story has actually *strengthened* (record backlog, diversification away from the Middle East, TPS quality), while the near-term earnings base took a genuine, exogenous hit.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Strong balance sheet… significant net cash" (every call) | Gross cash €4.8bn at mid-2026, but this sits against €4.1bn of customer advances (net contract liabilities). Management itself publishes the honest figure: economic net cash of roughly €900 million–€1 billion. | **Verified, with a caveat.** The often-quoted ~€2.9bn optical net cash triple-counts customer money; the real, unencumbered figure is ~€900M. Management is unusually candid about this. |
| "€800 million EBITDA by 2028… we are slightly ahead" | 2025 recurring EBITDA €638M (+5%). 2026 will fall well short after the war hit. Management reaffirms 2028 as "absolutely compatible." | **Credible but now war-contingent.** The trajectory was on track pre-conflict; the 2028 target survives only if the Middle East normalizes and cost recovery lands. |
| "Best-in-class Project Delivery margins" | Segment EBITDA margin ran ~8% through 2024-25, then collapsed to 4.3% in H1 2026. | **Broke on an exogenous shock, not on execution.** The cause is Hormuz logistics and provisions, and the rest of the (non-Middle-East) portfolio "is absolutely delivering." |
| "TPS is our higher-margin, faster-growth segment" | TPS margin climbed from ~12% to a record 15.4% in H1 2026 (+30bps YoY), fully offsetting a 2% revenue dip; but TPS *revenue* fell ~9% in 2025 and backlog is only ~€1.5bn. | **Half-right.** The margin story is real and improving; the growth story stalled (ethylene down-cycle), now leaning on AM&C and carbon-capture products to re-accelerate. |
| "Consistent 70-85% free-cash-flow conversion" | H1 2026 free-cash conversion (ex-working-capital) held at 86%; actual FCF €183M, down on lower EBITDA. | **Verified.** Cash generation held up even as reported profit fell — a genuine quality marker. |
| "Cost recovery under strong contractual protection" | Provisions taken; "some customers have already signed off," booked at cost (dilutive); the majority "is recoverable and should be recovered" but is **not yet recognized**. | **Unproven and prudent.** Management deliberately excluded unsigned recoveries — the honest choice, but it means the upside is real yet undated. |

Where the story is *richer than the numbers*: the 2028 €800M EBITDA target and 2027 "meaningful recovery." Where it is *poorer than the numbers suggest at a glance*: the optical net cash and free-cash-flow yield, which are inflated by customer advances.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable, with a defensive shift in the near term.**

- FY2024 (2025-02-27): peak confidence — "outstanding," "stellar," "highest-ever," near-50% dividend hike. Offensive.
- Q1 2025 (2025-04-30): still confident but hedging — "we have widened the revenue range… considering some of the macro movements… just in case."
- H1/9M 2025: measured; leaning on backlog coverage and TPS margins; green hydrogen openly labelled "a bit of a disappointment."
- FY2025 (2026-02-26): confident again on a record year and the NFW win.
- H1 2026 (2026-07-30): candid and defensive — "clearly disappointing," "we acknowledge the setback," repeated insistence on being "nonspeculative and prudent." Notably, management did *not* reach for optimism it could not sign for; the CEO refused to quantify potential margin upside because the recovery agreements were not yet inked.

The confidence about the *long-term* portfolio never wavered; the humility is confined to the war-hit near term. That pattern — owning the miss plainly while refusing to book unearned recovery — reads as credible rather than evasive.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** The company confirmed its full-year 2025 guidance at every 2025 call and delivered a record year. It has a habit of raising the pillar it can see (Project Delivery in Q1 2025, TPS margin in H2 2025 and again in H1 2026) while widening ranges on the pillar it cannot (short-cycle TPS revenue). The one large miss — the H1 2026 Project Delivery margin cut — was driven by an act of war (the Strait of Hormuz closure), not by an execution failure or a credibility gap, and management provisioned it prudently rather than smoothing it. The screener's 50% earnings-beat rate (3 of 6 quarters) is unremarkable, but the misses have been small and macro-driven, not narrative-driven. Against the tendency of E&C contractors to hide cost overruns until they explode, Technip Energies' transparency here is a positive.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Cost-recovery quantum and timing** (Rothschild, Kepler, Morgan Stanley, H1 2026): analysts pressed repeatedly for how much of the €30-40 million-per-quarter logistics hit is recoverable and when. Management would only say "a very small minority" is baked into guidance and signatures are coming "in the weeks to come" — a genuine non-answer on the number that matters most.
- **Order-intake phasing into 2027-28** (Barclays, Jefferies): analysts noted that of €13bn booked year-to-date, only ~€1bn is scheduled into 2027 revenue, questioning how fast the record backlog converts. Management pointed to war-driven phasing uncertainty.
- **LNG oversupply** (recurring since mid-2025): analysts worry about a 2028 LNG glut; management deflects to a "supply-led, long-cycle" framing and a "900 million tonnes by mid-next-decade" demand number.
- **Reju / adjacent bets**: analysts consistently probe the cash going into Reju; management caps it (~€50M/year) and frames it as optional.

The topic analysts pushed on that *became* the bad news: geopolitical/Middle East risk, flagged softly from Q1 2025, which detonated in H1 2026.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The near-term earnings base is hostage to one exogenous factor** — the Strait of Hormuz. Management's own base case assumes the disruption "persists throughout the year," and the top line could fall "if things were worsening."
🔴 **Cost recovery is real but undated and unsigned for the majority** — booked-at-cost even where signed (dilutive), and the "weeks to come" language has a whiff of the serially-deferred.
🔴 **Optical cheapness is misleading** — the ~€2.9bn net cash and ~25% free-cash-flow yield are inflated by customer advances; the honest figures (~€900M net cash) are far less dramatic.
🔴 **Higher tax rate (30-32%)** and elevated corporate costs (€65-70M) compress 2026 net income further.

🟢 **Record €25 billion backlog (+50% year-to-date), ~3x revenue** — the strongest visibility in company history, ~75% sourced outside the Middle East over 24 months.
🟢 **TPS margin at a record 15.4%** and structurally improving via AM&C (catalysts, ~70% OpEx-linked recurring revenue).
🟢 **Genuine net-cash balance sheet** funding a €1.00 dividend, a completed €150M buyback, and ~€300M of 2026 shareholder returns (~5% of market cap).
🟢 **Cash conversion held at 86%** through the profit trough.
🟢 **Management candour** — the war hit was owned, quantified where possible, and prudently provisioned.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **"Energy addition," not "energy transition."** The CEO's language has shifted toward energy security and supply diversification — "GCC countries… reducing reliance on the Strait of Hormuz… fast-tracking pipelines and export hubs." The war is being reframed as a *demand catalyst* for new infrastructure (alternative export routes, fast-track projects), which is where the €12.7bn order surge partly comes from.
- **Diversification is now the headline defence.** The "75% of orders outside the Middle East" statistic, once a footnote, is now the CEO's first answer to any Middle East risk question.
- **Capital allocation maturing.** From "dividend growth" (2024) to disciplined M&A (AM&C) plus a buyback plus a new €500M bond raised "for general corporate purposes" — the balance sheet is being put to work, not just admired.
- **A new adjacent bet appeared quietly:** a sustainable-aviation-fuel joint venture with Airbus, Safran and Tereos, sitting alongside Reju as optional long-term optionality.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.** The durable earnings engine is intact and, on the commercial side, stronger than ever; the 2026 profit shock is exogenous, transitory in management's framing, and backed by contractual cost-recovery rights and a fortress-adjacent (net-cash) balance sheet.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is, right now, a levered bet on the Strait of Hormuz reopening and on cost-recovery agreements getting signed. The recovery thesis is *not* independent of the single dominant macro factor the committee is most exposed to. The upside (a re-rate as margins normalize toward the reaffirmed €800M 2028 EBITDA framework) is real but undated; the downside is a war that drags into 2027 and keeps Project Delivery margins pinned near 5%. The discount to a fair reckoning of intrinsic value is only modest (~10-15%), so this is a quality franchise at a fair-to-slightly-cheap price with a live geopolitical overhang — not a deep, clean bargain.

**Economic moat: NARROW, trend STABLE.** The durable advantages are proprietary LNG and carbon-capture technology (intangible/IP), incumbency on the Qatar North Field complex (NFE/NFS/NFW) that compounds into follow-on awards, and a negative-working-capital model that makes the business self-funding. These are real but not impregnable — this is a competitive-bid E&C market (Saipem, Worley, KBR, Chiyoda, JGC). The core-margin compression is exogenous (war), not erosion; TPS margins are actually *widening*, which is why the moat trend is stable rather than eroding.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The obvious worry — a long-term decline in gas/LNG demand under the energy transition — cuts the other way here: Technip Energies is positioned as a transition *winner* (carbon capture, blue/green molecules, sustainable fuels, LNG as coal-displacement and data-center power). A 2028+ LNG oversupply is a cyclical risk to award timing, not a terminal-value threat to the franchise. The cheapness is therefore a fear-print around a war and a profit trough, not a structurally shrinking base — but the margin of safety is thin enough that discipline, not enthusiasm, is warranted.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable
